title: Alabama Child Custody Laws: How Courts Decide (2026 Guide)
excerpt: A practical, statute-based guide to Alabama child custody: joint vs. sole custody, best-interest factors under Ala. Code § 30-3-152, parenting plans, and what proposed 2025–2026 bills did (and did not) change.
author: A Mark
content:
Alabama custody cases turn on one central question: what arrangement serves the best interest of the child? This guide explains how Alabama courts currently evaluate custody under the Code of Alabama, what “joint custody” means in practice, how parents can prepare, and how recent legislative proposals fit into the picture—without treating failed bills as enacted law.

This article is general information about Alabama family-law procedures. It is not legal advice. Custody outcomes depend on the facts of each case and the court applying current statutes and case law. Consult a licensed Alabama family-law attorney for advice about your situation.

What “custody” means in Alabama

Alabama courts typically separate two related concepts:

  • Legal custody — authority to make major decisions about education, medical care, religion, and similar issues.
  • Physical custody — where the child lives and the day-to-day parenting schedule.

Either form can be joint (shared between parents) or sole (primarily with one parent). Joint physical custody does not always mean a 50/50 overnight split; it means both parents have substantial periods of physical custody under a workable schedule.

Current law: Ala. Code § 30-3-152

Under Alabama Code § 30-3-152, the court must consider joint custody in every case, but it may award any custody arrangement that is in the child’s best interest.

When deciding whether joint custody is appropriate, the statute directs courts to weigh the same factors used for sole custody decisions, plus factors such as:

  • Whether the parents agree (or disagree) on joint custody
  • Each parent’s past and present ability to cooperate and make decisions together
  • Each parent’s willingness to support the child’s relationship with the other parent
  • Any history or risk of child abuse, spouse abuse, or kidnapping
  • Geographic proximity and practical logistics of shared physical custody

The court may order a form of joint custody even without both parents’ consent when joint custody serves the child’s best interest.

When there is a statutory presumption

Alabama law currently creates a presumption favoring joint custody only when both parents request joint custody. In that situation, joint custody is presumed to be in the child’s best interest unless the court makes specific findings explaining why it is not granted.

If the parents do not both request joint custody, there is no automatic statewide presumption that equal parenting time is the default. The court still considers joint custody, but the outcome is driven by best-interest evidence.

Proposed bills vs. enacted law (important 2025–2026 update)

Readers often see headlines about a “joint custody presumption” in Alabama. Here is the accurate status as of 2026:

  • 2025 HB 229 (often described as a Best Interest of the Child Protection Act / joint-custody presumption bill) was introduced but did not become law; it died in committee without enactment.
  • 2026 HB 147 revived similar joint-custody presumption language and also did not become law.

Until the Legislature enacts a new statute signed into law, Alabama custody decisions continue under existing Code provisions such as § 30-3-152—not under the text of failed bills. Always verify the current Code of Alabama and recent appellate decisions before relying on any summary.

How Alabama courts evaluate the child’s best interest

Beyond the joint-custody factors above, Alabama courts look at the whole parenting picture. Evidence commonly includes:

  • Each parent’s ability to provide a stable, safe home
  • The emotional ties between the child and each parent
  • Each parent’s capacity to meet educational, medical, and developmental needs
  • Any history of domestic violence, substance abuse, or neglect
  • The child’s adjustment to home, school, and community
  • In appropriate cases, the preferences of a child who is mature enough to express them

No single factor controls every case. Judges weigh the evidence presented through testimony, documents, guardian ad litem reports (when appointed), and court-ordered evaluations.

Preparing for a custody case in Alabama

1. Organize records early

Useful documentation often includes school and medical records, calendars showing caregiving time, communication logs, proof of income and housing stability, and evidence related to safety concerns when relevant. Keep records factual and dated.

2. Draft a realistic parenting plan

A parenting plan should address the residential schedule (including holidays and school breaks), decision-making authority, transportation, communication methods, and how disputes will be handled. Courts favor plans that a child can follow consistently and that reduce conflict.

3. Focus on co-parenting capacity

Alabama’s statutory factors place real weight on cooperation and supporting the child’s relationship with the other parent. Hostile emails, withheld parenting time without a safety basis, or refusal to share important information can undermine a custody position.

4. Get Alabama-specific legal counsel

Local practice, temporary orders, mediation requirements, and county procedures vary. An attorney licensed in Alabama can explain filing venues, temporary relief, and how evidence is typically presented in your circuit.

Practical co-parenting tips that help children—and cases

  • Use written, civil communication for scheduling and major decisions
  • Keep the child out of adult conflict and legal strategy
  • Follow temporary orders precisely until they are modified
  • Propose solutions that protect school stability and the child’s routines
  • Document compliance with support, medical appointments, and exchanges

Finding the right Alabama court

Custody cases are generally handled in the circuit court (often through a domestic relations or family division) where the family has the required connections under Alabama venue rules. Use our court directory or court search to locate courthouse addresses, phone numbers, and related court information while you prepare filings with counsel.

Key takeaways

  • Alabama requires courts to consider joint custody in every case under § 30-3-152.
  • A statutory presumption favoring joint custody applies when both parents request it—not as a universal equal-time default.
  • Major 2025–2026 presumption bills (including HB 229 and HB 147) did not become law.
  • Preparation, credible evidence, and a child-focused parenting plan matter more than internet summaries of proposed legislation.

Laws and court practices change. Confirm the current Code of Alabama and seek personalized advice from a licensed attorney before taking legal action.

faqs.question: Does Alabama have a joint custody presumption in every case?
faqs.answer: No. Under Ala. Code § 30-3-152, courts must consider joint custody in every case, but a presumption favoring joint custody applies when both parents request it. Proposed bills that would have created a broader presumption (including 2025 HB 229 and 2026 HB 147) did not become law.

faqs.question: What is the difference between legal and physical custody in Alabama?
faqs.answer: Legal custody covers major decisions such as education and medical care. Physical custody covers where the child lives and the parenting-time schedule. Either can be joint or sole.

faqs.question: Did Alabama HB 229 change custody law in 2026?
faqs.answer: No. HB 229 did not become law. Related 2026 legislation (HB 147) also did not become law. Current custody analysis still follows existing Alabama Code provisions such as § 30-3-152.
